Most systems have all outputs wired to the Intel GPU to preserve battery life at times when you might be using an external display/projector on battery power. the initial wave of VR headsets used HDMI.  Some still do.  However, the new Oculus Rift S switched over to DisplayPort.  DisplayPort video output can be achieved from a USB-C port that supports video output by using a USB-C to DisplayPort dongle.  However, on every Dell system I'm aware of that has a USB-C port that supports video output, the USB-C port's video interface is wired to the Intel GPU.  The only exceptions I know of are the Precision 7000 Series models from the xx20 onward, which have a BIOS option that allows you to choose which GPU controls the display outputs.  They achieve that with a more complex and expensive motherboard design, but I haven't seen that implemented elsewhere.So if you're trying for VR, you might have to give some thought to which VR headset you want to use, because if you have a system where only the HDMI output is wired to the discrete GPU, then you can't use a DisplayPort-based VR headset.  There are DisplayPort to HDMI adapters, but they don't work in that direction.  They can only convert a DisplayPort source to an HDMI signal, not the other way around. There's also a new standard called VirtualLink that is backed by all major VR headset and GPU manufacturers that is basically a new way to configure a USB-C interface to carry enough power, video, and data to run an entire VR headset from a single cable.  It's expected to be used on future VR headsets.  I may be wrong here, but I don't think it will be possible to retrofit VirtualLink support to existing systems because VirtualLink basically involves running USB 3.0 traffic over pins on the USB-C connector that the current spec reserves for USB 2.0 (in order to increase available video bandwidth by reconfiguring the typical USB 3.0 pins for video).  That said, I don't know of 67,"@michaelmass  I know it would work with them in the sense that you can send a picture to them, but my understanding is that you wouldn't be able to use the actual G-Sync feature with them.  The Dell D6000 uses DisplayLink (not to be confused with DisplayPORT), and due to a Windows limitation, that means that on systems with both Intel and NVIDIA GPUs active, you can't even use the NVIDIA GPU's graphical acceleration horsepower, because DisplayLink will only allow you to use the primary GPU, which in dual GPU systems will be the Intel GPU.  And G-Sync requires not only that the NVIDIA GPU be used, but that it have direct control of the display output connector.  On most laptops, the NVIDIA GPU doesn't have direct control of any outputs and instead works through NVIDIA Optimus as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the Intel GPU, which IS directly connected to the display outputs.  But DisplayLink in particular is an ""indirect display"" technology that involves compressing rendered video and transmitting it as regular USB data.  That's how the D6000 and other DisplayLink-based adapters and docks can support plugging into a system over USB-A, which has no native video output support.  So in that case, NEITHER of the system's GPUs would have direct control of the display output connector.If you're claiming that the D6000 supports G-Sync displays 67,"@Bobberuchi  Where are you finding that the P2415Q supports G-Sync?  I can't find that indicated anywhere, and it seems very unlikely given that the P Series is Dell's ""Professional"" line and is therefore focused on features that businesses care about, like built-in USB ports, height-adjustable stands, daisy chaining, etc. -- not gaming features like G-Sync.But assuming you did buy G-Sync displays, your ability to use it will depend on whether the GPU outputs exposed on the USB-C/TB3 port are wired to the Intel GPU or NVIDIA GPU.  If you want to find out, connect any display or TV to that port using something like a USB-C to DP/HDMI adapter or cable, then go to NVIDIA Control Panel > PhysX Configuration.
